title: Chapter VI

teacherSummary.text: Recovering, Victor reads a letter from Elizabeth telling of home and of Justine Moritz, a servant girl who became part of the family. Victor now hates natural philosophy. He and Clerval study languages and take a restorative walking tour.

vocabulary.context: We passed a fortnight in these perambulations: my health and spirits had long been restored, and they gained additional strength from the salubrious air I breathed, the natural incidents of our progress, and the conversation of my friend.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “salubrious”: -ious (Latin -iosus, "full of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: The pretty Miss Mansfield has already received the congratulatory visits on her approaching marriage with a young Englishman, John Melbourne, Esq.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “congratulatory”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ory (Latin -orius, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Krempe was not equally docile; and in my condition at that time, of almost insupportable sensitiveness, his harsh blunt encomiums gave me even more pain than the benevolent approbation of M.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “encomium”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: The poor woman was very vacillating in her repentance.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “vacillating”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I figure to myself that the task of attending on your sick bed has devolved on some mercenary old nurse, who could never guess your wishes, nor minister to them with the care and affection of your poor cousin.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “devolve”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Means or mode of expressing thoughts
vocabulary.context: I did not, like him, attempt a critical knowledge of their dialects, for I did not contemplate making any other use of them than temporary amusement.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “dialect”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Clerval, whose eyes and feelings were always quick in discerning the sensations of others, declined the subject, alleging, in excuse, his total ignorance; and the conversation took a more general turn.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “allege”: leg (Latin lex/legere, "law" / "to read, choose"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A slight natural depression or indentation on the surface of some part of the body, esp
vocabulary.context: When he smiles, two little dimples appear on each cheek, which are rosy with health.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “dimple”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Summer passed away in these occupations, and my return to Geneva was fixed for the latter end of autumn; but being delayed by several accidents, winter and snow arrived, the roads were deemed impassable, and my journey was retarded until the ensuing spring.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “retard”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + ard (Latin ardere, "to burn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Young men should be diffident of themselves, you know, M.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “diffident”: fid (Latin fides, "faith") + -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

context.history: Romantic writers believed nature could heal the mind, a theme in Wordsworth's poetry.

significance: The calm before tragedy: Justine's introduction sets up her later fate.
discussionQuestions: Why does Shelley introduce Justine through a cheerful letter?
Where does setting appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with creation and responsibility?

items.prompt: Who writes to Victor during his recovery?

options: A girl who became a servant and part of the family

items.prompt: How does Victor now feel about natural philosophy?

options: A walking tour in nature with Clerval

items.prompt: In the line “We passed a fortnight in these perambulations: my health and spirits had long been restored, and they gained additional strength from the salubrious air I breathed, the natural incidents of our progress, and the conversation of my friend.”, what does “salubrious” most nearly mean?

In the line “The pretty Miss Mansfield has already received the congratulatory visits on her approaching marriage with a young Englishman, John Melbourne, Esq.”, what does “congratulatory” most nearly mean?

answerKey.answer: A girl who became a servant and part of the family
A walking tour in nature with Clerval

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter VI,” how does Shelley show recovery and false peace? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the setting you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter VI, how does Shelley develop the idea of recovery and false peace? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the setting in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter VI develops the idea of recovery and false peace. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of setting and tone / mood shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter VI (where it begins, turns and ends) and its setting shape the reader's understanding of recovery and false peace. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter VI suggests about recovery and false peace. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's setting and tone / mood), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses setting in Chapter VI to complicate the reader's understanding of recovery and false peace. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter VI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of recovery and false peace responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter VI alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of recovery and false peace follows or bends those conventions, using the setting as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter VI and its treatment of recovery and false peace. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's setting and tone / mood, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter VI as evidence for a larger claim about recovery and false peace in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter VI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of recovery and false peace. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why does Shelley introduce Justine through a cheerful letter? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are salubrious, congratulatory, encomiums, vacillating, devolved. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “We passed a fortnight in these perambulations: my health and spirits had long been restored, and they gained additional strength from the salubrious air I breathed, the natural incidents of our progress, and the conversation of my friend.” Webster's says: Favorable to health. Now the word history: “salubrious”: -ious (Latin -iosus, "full of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “congratulatory”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ory (Latin -orius, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “encomium”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Romantic writers believed nature could heal the mind, a theme in Wordsworth's poetry. Why does this chapter matter? The calm before tragedy: Justine's introduction sets up her later fate. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for setting.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see setting, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to recovery and false peace.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Setting, Tone / mood, Characterization.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of setting. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “I must say also a few words to you, my dear cousin, of little darling William. I wish you could see him; he is very tall of his age, with sweet laughing blue eyes, dark eyelashes, and curling hair. When he smiles, two little dimples appear on each cheek, which are rosy with health. He has already had one or two little wives, but Louisa Biron is his favourite, a pretty little girl of five years of age.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Setting, Tone / mood, Characterization: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter VI,” how does Shelley show recovery and false peace? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the setting you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about recovery and false peace, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how setting shapes recovery and false peace. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
